title: Finding local customers without relying on bidding sites
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who want local, repeatable ways to find customers
learningOutcomes: Choose two or three local customer-finding methods that fit the service list and the owner's available time.
Plan a letterbox or property-agent approach that respects consent, council rules and privacy.
Track each enquiry to its source, and review which methods produced jobs after a set period.

instruction.heading: Why local methods still matter
instruction.body: Many enquiries come from people who live near the business or need the work done close to home. Online bidding sites put a business in competition with many others at once. Local methods allow a business to build a reputation in a small area, with fewer rivals for each job. These methods work best when the service list is clear (“Choosing your service list and checking local demand”) and the owner can respond quickly. Because local methods take time, choose two or three rather than trying everything at once.

instruction.heading: Letterbox drops and printed offers
instruction.body: A letterbox drop puts a printed offer into homes on a chosen street or in a chosen suburb. Use a clear photo of the owner's own completed work, a short list of services and one way to respond. Check whether the local council allows distribution, and respect any no junk mail sign on a letterbox. Track the number of letters delivered, the enquiries received and the jobs won, so the cost of each lead can be judged. Printed mail is not governed by the Spam Act 2003, but the content must still be accurate and must not imply a licence or an insurance cover the owner does not hold.

instruction.heading: Property managers, agents and strata contacts
instruction.body: Property managers, agents and strata managers often need small repairs done quickly, between tenancies or on common property. Introduce the business in person or by letter, bring a short service list, and offer a trial quote. Once the business holds insurance, provide a certificate when the agency asks for one. Agents usually have preferred trades and set their own contractor requirements, so follow those conditions. A lasting arrangement grows from reliable work and clear quotes, not from underpricing other trades.

instruction.heading: Vehicle signage, cards and a simple web page
instruction.body: Business cards work well when handed over at the end of a job, with the client's permission to give them out. A simple web page with a short service list, photos of the owner's own work used with consent, and a contact method is enough to begin. Keep the business details accurate, because enquiries will check them.

instruction.heading: Recording where each enquiry came from
instruction.body: Ask every caller how they found the business, and record the answer against the enquiry. After six to eight weeks, compare the enquiries, quotes and jobs for each method. Drop any method that produced no jobs, and put more time into the methods that did. This record helps the owner spend marketing money on what works.

procedure: Choose two or three local methods that match the service list and the time available.
Write a clear one-page offer with a service list, the owner's own photos and one way to respond.
Check council distribution rules and respect any no-junk-mail sign before delivering letters.
Contact property managers and agents with a short introduction and a trial quote offer, following their contractor requirements.
Record the source of every enquiry, quote and job.
Review the results after six to eight weeks, and keep, change or stop each method.

workedExamples.situation: An owner plans to deliver 200 letters in one suburb, with a photo of a deck repair and a phone number, and wants to measure the results.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must the owner check before delivering the letters?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should confirm the council distribution rules, respect any no-junk-mail signs, and check that the photo shows the owner's own work with the client's consent. The letter must not claim a licence or insurance the owner does not hold. The owner should also set up a way to tell which letters led to enquiries, so the cost per job can be calculated.

equipmentAndPpe: Printed offer with the service list, the owner's own photos and a tracking code
Enquiry log with a source column
Consent form for any client photo or name

commonErrors.error: Using a client's photo or name without consent.
commonErrors.prevention: Get written or recorded consent before any client photo or name is used, and keep the record.

commonErrors.error: Relying on one local method and stopping after a single attempt.
commonErrors.prevention: Test each method for a fixed period, then compare the results.

commonErrors.error: Claiming a licence or insurance cover the owner does not hold.
commonErrors.prevention: Check each claim against the business file before it is published.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Electronic marketing messages by email or SMS must follow the Spam Act 2003: consent, sender identification and a working unsubscribe option. The ACMA guidance checked on 2026-11-02 says unsubscribe requests must be acted on within five working days. Letters and in-person contact are not covered by that rule, but they must still be accurate.
Council rules on leaflet distribution, vehicle advertising and signage must be checked with the council or the state authority before use.
Client photos and names are personal information, and they are used only with consent. Nothing in this lesson grants a licence to advertise regulated work.

qualityStandard: Two or three methods are chosen with a reason, and each has an owner and a review date.
Every marketing item is checked for licence claims, consent and council rules.
Each enquiry is recorded with its source.
documentationEvidence: Written offer and distribution plan, with the council check recorded
Enquiry log showing the source of each enquiry, quote and job
Consent records for any client photo or name used
summary: Choose two or three local methods, and give each a fixed test period.
Check council rules, consent and licence claims before anything is published.
Track sources, so that spending follows results.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which action best supports a letterbox campaign?
options: Delivering letters without checking council rules and to every house on the street at once
Checking council distribution rules, respecting no-junk-mail signs, and recording which letters led to enquiries
Using a client's photo without asking and using the client's name and address in the letter
Claiming an insurance cover to build trust that the business does not hold yet and the licence too

knowledgeChecks.question: Which rule applies to a promotional email sent to past clients?
options: No rule applies, because the client knows the business and has used it before
Consent, sender identification and an unsubscribe option under the Spam Act 2003
Only the sender's home address must be shown and the sender's phone number
The message must be sent in a language the client chooses and sent only on weekdays

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should every enquiry be recorded with its source?
options: So the owner can avoid answering the phone and the calls can be left to voicemail
So marketing spending can be compared with the jobs each method produces
So customers can be charged more and the price for each job can rise
So licence claims can be published on every page of the website

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (Australian Communications and Media Authority)
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial electronic messages cannot be sent without permission or consent; sender identification must accurately name the business and its contact details, kept accurate for at least 30 days; messages must include a way to withdraw permission, and unsubscribe requests must be actioned within five business days. Does not cover council leaflet distribution or vehicle signage rules. Publisher: ACMA.
